content.text: Nap (short for Napoleon) is a classic English trick-taking game that gained massive popularity in Britain during the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is a quick, high-stakes game where players bid on how many of their five cards they can win in a trick-based battle against everyone else. Known for its escalating bidding tiers named after Napoleonic battles (Wellington, BlÃ¼cher) and its simple yet ruthless scoring system.

Napoleon is a classic English pub game first documented in H.E. Heather's October 1875 edition of The Bazaar. It quickly became England's national five-card game, displacing Loo. Early authors described it as 'spirited and interesting', requiring 'considerable judgement and skill'. The expression 'going Nap' (meaning to risk all on one attempt) derives from this game.
3-8 players; 4-5 is optimal. No permanent partnershipsâ€”high bidder plays against all others.
Standard 52-card pack. Cards rank A-K-Q-J-10-9-8-7-6-5-4-3-2. Often reduced: 3 players use 20 cards (A-K-Q-J-10), 4 players use 28 (A-8), 5 players use 32 (A-7).
Standard deck, poker chips or counters for stakes.
Five cards to each playerâ€”either 3 then 2, or 2 then 3. Cards are shuffled only at start and after successful Nap/Wellington/BlÃ¼cher bids; otherwise just gathered and cut.

items.text: Two Bid: Lowest bid at 2 tricks, worth 2 units. Ranking below Three.
MisÃ¨re (Mis): Bid to lose every trick. Fails if opponents force you to win a trick. Worth 3 points, ranks between Three and Four.
Peep Nap (Floater): Extra card dealt face-down to table. Players may pay to privately view it before bidding. Winner of Nap/Wellington/BlÃ¼cher also wins the pool.
Purchase Nap: Before bidding, players may pay to discard and draw replacement cards from undealt stock.
